faqs.answer: Better to bake it and freeze the baked cupcakes. Batter with baking powder or soda loses its lift sitting in the freezer, and thawed batter bakes flat. Baked cupcakes freeze well for weeks.

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 0.79. Factor = new area divided by old area = 50.3 divided by 63.6 = 0.79.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: An 8-inch round covers 50.3 square inches and a 9-inch round covers 63.6. Divide 50.3 by 63.6 and the factor is 0.79.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 0.79, including the leavening. A recipe with 5 cups of batter becomes 4 cups.

howToSteps.name: Bake the leftover separately
howToSteps.text: Pour the scaled batter into a greased 8-inch round pan, and bake the leftover batter as cupcakes or in a ramekin. Do not overfill the pan.

howToSteps.name: Bake as the recipe says
howToSteps.text: Same oven temperature, same bake time. Test with a toothpick at the recipe time.

title: 9-Inch Round to 8-Inch Round Pan
tutorial: Scaling down is the same maths as scaling up, run the other way. A 9-inch round covers 63.6 square inches and an 8-inch round covers 50.3, so the smaller pan holds about 21 percent less. The factor is 50.3 divided by 63.6, which is 0.79. A recipe that makes 5 cups of batter for a 9-inch layer becomes 4 cups for an 8-inch layer.

The 8-inch round holds 6 cups to the rim, against 8 cups for the 9-inch round. Two-thirds full in the 8-inch pan is 4 cups, which is exactly what a scaled 5-cup recipe gives you. The numbers line up neatly here, which is why this swap feels easy once the factor is known. Wilton agrees from the test kitchen: one 8-inch layer takes 4 cups of batter, one 9-inch layer takes 5.

Pour the full 9-inch recipe into the 8-inch pan and the batter sits about 26 percent deeper. It can still work if the pan is 2 inches deep and the fill stays under two-thirds, but expect 10 to 15 minutes longer in the oven and a domed top that needs trimming before stacking. King Arthur warns that more batter in a smaller pan takes longer to bake and risks a dry crumb or a slumped middle. Scaling is the better plan.

The leftover batter is not waste. A 5-cup recipe scaled to 4 cups leaves 1 cup over, and a cup of batter bakes into about four cupcakes, since one cupcake cup takes about a quarter cup of batter. Bake them alongside the cake layer and they come out a few minutes sooner, which makes them the cook's treat while the layer cools.

Bake at the same temperature and the same time. Both pans are 2 inches deep and the scaled batter sits at the same depth, so the middle sets on the same schedule. A smaller layer also needs less frosting: the top is about a fifth smaller, so make about a fifth less frosting, or keep the extra for the cupcakes.
